business_problem: Arup needed to evaluate far more structural design options early in projects so engineers could optimize performance, material use, and embodied carbon, but traditional FEM simulations were too slow and queue-bound to support near-real-time iteration.
solution_summary: Arup sped up its structural design workflow by replacing repeated full finite element method runs with graph neural network (GNN) surrogate models trained and deployed on NVIDIA DGX Spark. Engineers generate many building-massing or other structural options through parametric modeling, then use the GNN models to predict structural performance much faster than classical simulation so they can compare trade-offs earlier in the design cycle. DGX Spark supplies the local accelerated compute for both model execution and training, which lets Arup keep project data on site while shortening feedback loops from hours to minutes. The result is a practical two-stage architecture in which conventional FEM establishes the reference behavior, GNN surrogates provide fast iterative screening, and engineers use those AI-derived predictions to narrow the design space before making final structural decisions.

solution_components.name: Graph neural network (GNN) surrogate models
solution_components.role: Predict structural performance quickly enough for engineers to iterate through many low-carbon design options.

solution_components.name: NVIDIA DGX Spark
solution_components.role: Provides the local accelerated compute used to train and run the surrogate models in Arup's workflow.

data_flow: Arup generates structural options through parametric modeling, runs those options through GNN surrogate models on DGX Spark to predict performance in minutes, and uses the results to compare cost, carbon, and engineering trade-offs before narrowing designs for deeper analysis.
business_outcome: Arup reduced structural simulation evaluation from hours to minutes, achieved 90-95 percent accuracy against FEM baselines, and ran GNN execution and training up to 50 percent faster, allowing teams to make lower-carbon design decisions earlier and with better quantitative support.
